messages.content: I want to develop a subsurface two-phase flow surrogate that preserves local mass conservation while generalizing across unseen permeability connectivity. The targets are a maximum cellwise mass-balance error below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep and, on unseen channel connectivity, a breakthrough-time error below 5% versus a converged finite-volume solver.

That sets two distinct requirements for the surrogate. The mass-conservation target is local: at each timestep, even the cell with the largest mass-balance error must remain below 0.1% of the mass injected during that timestep. The generalization target concerns breakthrough timing when channel connectivity is unseen, with the surrogate’s error kept below 5% relative to the breakthrough time from a converged finite-volume solver. These are development targets, not claims that a surrogate has already achieved them.
When you say local, do you mean the 0.1% limit cannot be satisfied just by balancing errors across the domain?

Yes. A domain-wide balance could conceal positive and negative errors in different cells. A maximum cellwise limit instead concerns the worst cellwise mass-balance error, so cancellation across cells would not by itself satisfy it. The stated scale for that error is the injected mass per timestep, rather than, for example, the total mass injected over an entire run.
Is 0.1% an average over cells, then?

No. “Maximum cellwise mass-balance error” refers to the largest cellwise error. For the stated target, that maximum stays strictly below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep. An average below 0.1% would be a different condition and would not establish the requested maximum-error bound.
How should I understand the other target? Is it simply about matching flow behavior in familiar permeability patterns?

It is more specific than that. The breakthrough-time requirement applies on unseen channel connectivity: the surrogate is meant to retain timing accuracy when the way channels connect has not been seen. The comparison is to a converged finite-volume solver, and the permitted breakthrough-time error is strictly below 5% relative to that reference.
So a good mass-balance result alone would not settle the breakthrough-time requirement?

Correct. Keeping the maximum cellwise mass-balance error below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep would address the local-conservation target, but it would not, on its own, show that breakthrough-time error is below 5% on unseen channel connectivity. Both requirements matter to the stated goal.
And a close breakthrough time would not necessarily show local conservation either?

Right. Agreement on breakthrough time is a comparison of one predicted timing outcome with the converged finite-volume solver. It does not establish the worst-cell mass-balance error. The surrogate is intended to meet the local error bound while also meeting the breakthrough-time bound under the specified unseen-connectivity condition.
Does the wording require a particular surrogate architecture or a particular way of enforcing conservation?

No particular architecture or enforcement method is specified. The stated aim is to develop a subsurface two-phase flow surrogate with local mass conservation and generalization across unseen permeability connectivity, subject to those two numerical targets. The wording defines what performance is sought without selecting how to obtain it.
Does it specify exactly how breakthrough is detected?

No operational definition of breakthrough is supplied here. The requirement identifies breakthrough-time error, the unseen channel-connectivity condition, the below-5% threshold, and the converged finite-volume solver as the comparison baseline. It does not add a detection rule or other measurement details.
I want to make sure I am not conflating “unseen permeability connectivity” with merely changing permeability values.

That distinction is useful. The goal expressly concerns generalization across unseen permeability connectivity, and the breakthrough-time condition expressly mentions unseen channel connectivity. Those phrases emphasize unfamiliar connection patterns, not just a different numerical value in an otherwise familiar pattern. They do not, by themselves, specify which patterns or values are involved.
Can I describe the finite-volume result as the reference without claiming it is an exact physical truth?

Yes. The stated comparison is versus a converged finite-volume solver. Calling its breakthrough time the reference for the below-5% error target preserves that comparison without making a further claim that the solver represents exact physical truth.
Then the concise objective is a locally mass-conserving subsurface two-phase flow surrogate that handles unseen connectivity, with both numerical limits retained?

Yes: develop a subsurface two-phase flow surrogate that preserves local mass conservation while generalizing across unseen permeability connectivity. Its maximum cellwise mass-balance error should stay below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep, and its breakthrough-time error on unseen channel connectivity should remain below 5% versus a converged finite-volume solver.

For the surrogate, I propose using a permeability-conditioned graph network to predict face mobilities. We would then solve for pressure and update saturation using shared conservative finite-volume fluxes.

That proposal gives the learned component a specific role: it predicts face mobilities conditioned on permeability. Pressure is then solved, and saturation is updated using shared conservative finite-volume fluxes. In other words, the network is not being proposed as a direct predictor of the entire pressure and saturation evolution.
Why does predicting at faces matter in this description?

A finite-volume exchange between neighboring cells is represented at their shared face. Placing the mobility prediction there makes it available where the flux is formed. The proposal does not specify the network’s architecture or how it computes a face mobility; it specifies the quantity the network predicts and where that quantity enters the subsequent calculation.
What does “permeability-conditioned” add?

It says the graph network’s predictions depend on permeability, rather than being independent of it. That connects the learned mobility predictions to the permeability connectivity the surrogate is intended to handle. It does not, by itself, establish how well the network will generalize to connectivity it has not seen.
Could I describe the graph network as predicting the fluxes directly?

That would change the proposal. Here the network predicts face mobilities; the fluxes belong to the subsequent conservative finite-volume calculation used in the pressure solve and saturation update. Keeping those roles distinct is central to the proposed arrangement.
And pressure is still solved rather than simply output by the network?

Yes. “Solve pressure” identifies a separate pressure-solving step after the mobility prediction. The proposal does not specify the exact pressure equation, solver, or numerical tolerances, so it is best to leave those open rather than describe a particular implementation.
I want the pressure solve and saturation update to use shared fluxes. What does “shared” mean here?

It means the finite-volume fluxes are used consistently across those steps, rather than treating pressure and saturation as unrelated predictions with unrelated intercell exchanges. At an internal face, a conservative finite-volume treatment accounts for a shared exchange between the adjoining cells, with opposite contributions to their balances.
So one cell cannot gain mass from an internal face without the neighboring cell seeing the corresponding loss?

That is the conservation principle behind a shared internal-face flux: the exchange is accounted for on both sides of the same face. It explains why this construction is relevant to local mass conservation. It does not, without further specification or evaluation, prove that every cellwise mass-balance error will meet the goal’s numerical limit.
Is the saturation update a separate learned prediction too?

Not as stated. The proposal says to update saturation with shared conservative finite-volume fluxes. The learned prediction explicitly identified is the face mobility; describing a separate learned saturation predictor would add something the proposal does not specify.
How should I explain the order of operations without committing to extra details?

You can state the order already present: use a permeability-conditioned graph network to predict face mobilities, solve pressure, and update saturation with shared conservative finite-volume fluxes. That expresses the proposed division of work without specifying a particular time-stepping scheme, graph construction, or solver.
Would it be accurate to say the graph network itself enforces local conservation?

That would be too strong based on this proposal. The conservation-oriented part is the use of shared conservative finite-volume fluxes when solving pressure and updating saturation. The graph network supplies mobility predictions; the proposal does not say that its outputs alone enforce a cellwise mass balance.
Does calling the fluxes conservative mean the local mass-balance target is already met?

No. It identifies a proposed mechanism for preserving conservation, not a measured result. Whether the complete surrogate meets the specified maximum cellwise error bound would still have to be established; the proposal itself provides no error measurement.
What about the breakthrough-time target on unseen channel connectivity—does the graph network establish that?

No demonstrated breakthrough-time accuracy follows from choosing a permeability-conditioned graph network. Conditioning the mobility predictions on permeability is relevant to the generalization goal, but the proposal does not report performance on unseen channel connectivity or a comparison with the converged finite-volume solver.
Then the idea is partly learned and partly a finite-volume calculation?

Yes. As proposed, learning supplies the face mobilities, while pressure solving and saturation updating retain shared conservative finite-volume fluxes. That division is the defining feature here; it avoids claiming that the network directly supplies the final flow fields or that the proposed combination has already met either performance target.
Is “shared” referring only to the pressure and saturation steps, or also to the two cells next to a face?

Both readings help explain the proposed conservation structure without adding a new algorithm. The pressure solve and saturation update use shared finite-volume fluxes, and a conservative internal-face flux represents the same exchange in the balances of its adjacent cells. The proposal does not specify further details about how particular fluxes are calculated.
Could the description stay agnostic about the exact mobility definition?

Yes. “Face mobilities” is the specified prediction target. Nothing here fixes a particular mobility formula, a particular set of inputs beyond permeability conditioning, or a particular way of representing the two phases within the network. Those details need not be supplied to describe the proposal faithfully.
Please phrase the proposal in one sentence without turning its intended advantages into results.

Use a permeability-conditioned graph network to predict face mobilities, then solve pressure and update saturation with shared conservative finite-volume fluxes, as a proposed way to support local conservation and generalization across unseen permeability connectivity.
Does face-mobility learning keep breakthrough-time error below 5% on unseen channel connectivity when pressure and saturation use conservative finite-volume updates?

That is the question to establish, not a result we can infer from the proposal alone. Conservative finite-volume updates address how fluxes are accounted for, but they do not by themselves show that learned face mobilities produce a breakthrough time within 5% of the converged finite-volume solver on unseen channel connectivity.
Why wouldn’t conservative updates settle the timing question?

Conservation concerns the accounting of flow between cells. Breakthrough time also depends on the flow represented by those fluxes. If the learned face mobilities lead to different fluxes, a conservative update can still produce a different breakthrough time. Consistent accounting and accurate timing are related concerns, but they are not interchangeable.
So the phrase “with conservative finite-volume updates” is a condition on the question, not the answer?

Exactly. The question is whether face-mobility learning achieves breakthrough-time error below 5% on unseen channel connectivity *while using* conservative finite-volume updates. The presence of those updates does not imply that the error threshold has been met.
What specifically is being judged by the 5% threshold?

The quantity being judged is breakthrough-time error. In the stated goal, that error is compared with the breakthrough time from a converged finite-volume solver. The threshold is strictly below 5%, and it applies on unseen channel connectivity—not merely on connectivity the surrogate has already encountered.
Would demonstrating accurate breakthrough on familiar connectivity answer it?

No. It might say something about behavior on familiar connectivity, but this question expressly concerns unseen channel connectivity. Accuracy under a different connectivity condition would not establish the specified below-5% result.
Is the question asking whether face-mobility learning helps, or whether it actually meets the bound?

It asks whether the approach keeps breakthrough-time error below 5% under the stated condition. Saying the approach is relevant to that goal is weaker than showing it meets the bound. No measured breakthrough-time errors are provided here, so the bound remains an open question.
Could I answer yes just because the graph network is conditioned on permeability?

No. Permeability conditioning tells us what the mobility prediction responds to; it does not establish accuracy when channel connectivity is unseen. Nor does it establish the resulting breakthrough-time error relative to the converged finite-volume solver.
What role do the predicted face mobilities play in this question?

They are the learned part whose effect on breakthrough timing is at issue. In the proposed arrangement, the predicted face mobilities feed into the pressure solve and the shared conservative finite-volume fluxes used to update saturation. The question is whether that arrangement retains sufficiently accurate breakthrough timing on unseen channel connectivity.
If the fluxes are shared and conservative, could the learned mobilities still be the source of a timing difference?

Conceptually, yes. Sharing a flux ensures that an internal-face exchange is accounted for consistently by the neighboring cells. It does not require the magnitude or timing of that exchange to match the finite-volume reference when the mobility supplied to the calculation is learned. That is why breakthrough-time accuracy remains a separate question.
Does “below 5%” allow a result of exactly 5%?

No. Read literally, “below 5%” is a strict threshold: an error equal to 5% would not be below it. The question is whether the breakthrough-time error remains on the lower side of that boundary for the specified unseen channel-connectivity condition.
Am I asking whether the conservative update alone generalizes to unseen channels?

Not quite. The question concerns face-mobility learning *with* conservative finite-volume updates. It asks about breakthrough-time accuracy for the combined arrangement on unseen channel connectivity; it does not isolate the updates as a standalone predictor of breakthrough.
And I shouldn’t treat conservation as evidence of the 5% timing result?

Right. Conservative updates explain how the method handles flux accounting. Whether the learned mobilities, pressure solve, and saturation updates together keep breakthrough-time error below 5% on unseen channel connectivity must be determined from that timing comparison; conservation alone does not answer it.
What is the most precise way to leave the issue open?

Ask: “With face mobilities learned from permeability and pressure and saturation updated through shared conservative finite-volume fluxes, does breakthrough-time error on unseen channel connectivity stay below 5% versus a converged finite-volume solver?” That states the approach, the condition, and the comparison without claiming an outcome.
My hypothesis is that, on ChannelShift-2D, conservative updates with graph-predicted face mobilities yield less than 5% maximum breakthrough-time error across unseen channel topologies.

That is a testable hypothesis, not an observed result. It predicts that the largest breakthrough-time error across the unseen channel topologies on ChannelShift-2D will be strictly below 5%. The proposed combination is graph-predicted face mobilities with conservative updates; the breakthrough-time comparison remains against the converged finite-volume solver identified in the question.
Does “maximum” make this a stronger claim than saying the typical error is below 5%?

Yes. A typical or average error below 5% could coexist with an unseen topology whose error exceeds 5%. The hypothesis instead places the below-5% bound on the maximum breakthrough-time error across the unseen channel topologies under consideration.
So if one of those topologies has an error of 5% or more, would that contradict the hypothesis?

Yes, for the topologies being evaluated: a maximum cannot be below 5% if any included breakthrough-time error is 5% or higher. An error of exactly 5% would not satisfy the strict “less than 5%” wording.
Should I describe the hypothesis as applying to unseen permeability connectivity in general?

The hypothesis is more specifically framed: it applies on ChannelShift-2D and concerns unseen channel topologies. That is relevant to the broader connectivity goal, but the statement does not claim the same maximum-error bound for every possible permeability configuration or setting outside ChannelShift-2D.
What does naming ChannelShift-2D establish here?

It identifies the setting in which the hypothesis is made. The name alone does not supply a dataset size, a particular collection of topologies, or any measured errors, so none of those details should be inferred from it.
Could I say that conservative updates guarantee the timing bound?

No. The hypothesis predicts the bound for conservative updates used with graph-predicted face mobilities. Conservative flux accounting does not, by itself, guarantee an accurate breakthrough time. The accuracy of the learned mobilities’ contribution remains part of what the hypothesis puts at issue.
I also don’t want the wording to imply the graph predicts breakthrough time directly.

Then keep the roles explicit: the graph predicts face mobilities, conservative updates use the resulting flow calculation, and breakthrough-time error is the outcome whose maximum is hypothesized to stay below 5%. The hypothesis does not describe a graph that directly outputs breakthrough time.
Is this a statement about the mass-balance target too?

No. Although the updates are described as conservative, this particular hypothesis specifies a maximum *breakthrough-time* error below 5% on ChannelShift-2D across unseen channel topologies. It does not assert a measured maximum cellwise mass-balance error or establish the separate 0.1% mass-balance target.
How should I distinguish the maximum from an error calculated for each timestep?

Here “maximum” modifies breakthrough-time error across unseen channel topologies. Breakthrough time is the timing outcome being compared with the finite-volume reference; the hypothesis is not phrased as a per-timestep error bound. The per-timestep language belongs to the separate mass-balance requirement.
Could the hypothesis hold if several topologies are well below 5% but the worst one is just above it?

No. Even if most errors were well below 5%, a worst-case error above 5% would put the maximum above the threshold. The maximum, rather than the number of comparatively accurate cases, determines whether this hypothesis holds for the evaluated unseen topologies.
Am I already claiming evidence by saying “yield less than 5%”?

Not when it is clearly introduced as a hypothesis. The sentence states a predicted outcome to be assessed; it should not be reported as a finding without breakthrough-time comparisons. Keeping words such as “hypothesize” or “predict” makes that status clear.
Can you restate the hypothesis while preserving that uncertainty?

We hypothesize that, on ChannelShift-2D, conservative updates with graph-predicted face mobilities will keep the maximum breakthrough-time error strictly below 5% across unseen channel topologies, relative to a converged finite-volume solver. Whether that prediction holds has not been established by the hypothesis itself.

I plan to train on ChannelShift-2D straight and sinuous channels, then test on held-out branching connectivity. I want to compare breakthrough times with a converged finite-volume solver and examine cellwise residuals.

That separates the training and test connectivity in a specific way: straight and sinuous channels are used for training, while branching connectivity is held out for testing. The test examines breakthrough times against converged finite-volume results and cellwise residuals. It is a plan for assessing the surrogate, not a report of how it performs.
What is the significance of holding out the branching connectivity?

It makes branching connectivity the unseen-connectivity condition for this test. The comparison can then address how the surrogate behaves on that held-out connectivity rather than only on the straight and sinuous channels used for training. The plan does not specify how many branching cases are held out or how they are constructed.
Does the plan say to train on breakthrough times from the finite-volume solver?

No. It says to train on ChannelShift-2D straight and sinuous channels and to test held-out branching connectivity against converged finite-volume breakthrough times and cellwise residuals. It does not specify the training targets, loss, or other training details.
Then what exactly is the finite-volume solver doing in the stated test?

Its converged breakthrough times provide the reference for the breakthrough-time comparison. Calling them a reference does not imply that the plan specifies a convergence criterion or that the solver’s results are exact physical truth.
Are the cellwise residuals just another way of stating the breakthrough-time error?

No. Breakthrough-time error concerns a timing outcome relative to the converged finite-volume reference. Cellwise residuals concern what happens locally in the cells and are relevant to assessing the conservation aspect of the surrogate. Looking at both avoids treating agreement on breakthrough time as a substitute for examining local balance.
Should I say that the plan has already shown the maximum cellwise mass-balance error is below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep?

No. The plan calls for examining cellwise residuals; it provides no residual values. To assess the stated mass-balance target, the relevant quantity is the maximum cellwise mass-balance error, which must stay below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep. That target should not be presented as an outcome of a test that has only been planned.
Similarly, can I claim less than 5% breakthrough-time error on held-out branching connectivity?

Not yet. The plan provides the held-out connectivity and the converged finite-volume breakthrough times for the comparison, but no measured breakthrough-time errors. Whether the error stays below 5% remains to be determined by that comparison.
Why specify both straight and sinuous channels for training instead of saying only ‘train on ChannelShift-2D’?

Naming straight and sinuous channels makes the intended training connectivity explicit. It also makes clear what differs from the held-out branching connectivity used for testing. The broader phrase ‘train on ChannelShift-2D’ would leave that distinction unstated.
Does ‘held-out branching connectivity’ mean all possible branching arrangements are covered?

No. It identifies the kind of connectivity withheld for the test, but it does not specify the number or range of branching arrangements. Results from such a test would need to be described in terms of the branching connectivity actually evaluated, rather than automatically extended to every possible unseen topology.
If I report an average breakthrough-time error across the held-out cases, would that answer the maximum-error question?

An average alone would not establish a maximum-error bound. To assess whether breakthrough-time error stays below 5% across the tested held-out branching connectivity, the individual errors—and consequently their maximum—matter. The plan specifies the comparison but does not report either an average or a maximum.
For the cellwise residuals, why does it matter that they are cellwise rather than just one domain-wide number?

A domain-wide number can obscure an imbalance concentrated in a particular cell. Examining cellwise residuals keeps the local behavior visible, which is important when the goal is expressed as a maximum cellwise mass-balance error. The plan does not specify a residual calculation, so that distinction is about what the proposed examination is meant to reveal, not a claim about its result.
Should the test be described as a comparison of the learned face mobilities themselves with finite-volume mobilities?

That is not what this plan specifies. The proposed test concerns held-out branching connectivity, breakthrough times relative to converged finite-volume results, and cellwise residuals. It does not call for a separate face-mobility comparison.
Does using conservative finite-volume updates remove the need to look at cellwise residuals?

No. Conservative updates describe the proposed way of accounting for fluxes, while examining cellwise residuals checks the local balance in the resulting calculation. The plan retains that examination rather than assuming the update structure alone establishes a particular numerical error bound.
Can I describe this as a generalization test without implying it establishes generalization everywhere?

Yes. It is a generalization test in the specific sense that training uses straight and sinuous ChannelShift-2D channels and testing uses held-out branching connectivity. That description does not claim performance on connectivity outside the test or in settings beyond ChannelShift-2D.
What remains unspecified in the test description?

It does not state the number of cases, the exact train–test split, the training procedure, how breakthrough is detected, how residuals are calculated, or the solver’s convergence criterion. Those details should not be filled in as though the plan had supplied them. The stated plan is still clear about the training channel types, the held-out connectivity, and the two kinds of test quantities.
Could you restate the plan without turning the targets into findings?

Train the surrogate on ChannelShift-2D straight and sinuous channels, then test it on held-out branching connectivity by comparing breakthrough times against a converged finite-volume solver and examining cellwise residuals. The comparison is intended to assess the timing and local-balance targets; the plan does not state that either target has been met.
Run 100 held-out ChannelShift-2D branching cases, and compare breakthrough-time errors and injected-mass-normalized cellwise residuals against converged finite-volume solutions.

The activity is to evaluate 100 held-out ChannelShift-2D branching cases. For those cases, compare breakthrough times with converged finite-volume solutions to obtain breakthrough-time errors, and examine cellwise residuals normalized by injected mass against those solutions. This specifies the evaluation to carry out; it does not provide its results.
Does the number 100 refer to timesteps or cells?
Neither. It is the number of held-out ChannelShift-2D branching cases to run. The activity does not specify how many timesteps or cells any case contains.
Why keep “held-out” in the description?

It identifies the branching cases as the evaluation cases withheld from training. That distinction matters when examining behavior on unseen branching connectivity. It does not, by itself, say anything about the errors those cases will produce.
What does the converged finite-volume solution serve as here?

It is the reference for the comparisons in the activity. Breakthrough-time errors are assessed against the converged finite-volume results, and the injected-mass-normalized cellwise residuals are examined against those solutions. No particular solver settings or convergence criterion are specified.
Are breakthrough-time errors and cellwise residuals interchangeable measures?

No. Breakthrough-time error concerns the timing of breakthrough relative to the reference. A cellwise residual concerns local balance in a cell; normalizing it by injected mass expresses it on the stated mass scale. Looking at one does not replace examining the other.
Does “injected-mass-normalized” mean I should report only one residual for each branching case?

No. “Cellwise” retains the local character of the residuals. Normalization by injected mass changes their scale; it does not turn them into a single domain-wide residual. The activity does not prescribe a particular summary statistic for reporting them.
Can I say the 100 cases establish that the maximum breakthrough-time error is below 5%?

Not from the activity description alone. It specifies 100 cases and a breakthrough-time comparison, but gives no error values. The maximum across the evaluated cases can be assessed once their errors are available; it cannot be asserted from the case count.
Would looking only at the average error across the 100 cases address a maximum-error question?

No. An average can be low even when one case has a larger error. If the question concerns the maximum breakthrough-time error across these held-out cases, the largest of their individual errors is the relevant quantity. No average or maximum is reported here.
Could a small breakthrough-time error make the residual comparison unnecessary?

No. The activity calls for both comparisons because timing agreement does not establish the cellwise residuals. Even if a breakthrough time were close to its finite-volume reference, local balance would remain a separate quantity to examine.
And does normalizing the residuals by injected mass show that they meet the local mass-balance limit?

Normalization makes the residuals comparable on an injected-mass scale, but it does not state their magnitudes. Whether the maximum cellwise mass-balance error stays below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep depends on the residuals obtained, not on the choice to normalize them.
Should I describe these as 100 newly observed successes?

No. The activity says to run 100 held-out branching cases and make the specified comparisons. It supplies neither measured errors nor pass–fail outcomes, so describing the cases as successes would add a result that is not stated.
What would be a faithful short description of what is being done?

Evaluate 100 held-out ChannelShift-2D branching cases by comparing breakthrough-time errors and injected-mass-normalized cellwise residuals against converged finite-volume solutions, without presuming the outcomes of those comparisons.
Across the 100 held-out ChannelShift-2D branching cases, the maximum breakthrough-time error was 4.3%, and the maximum cellwise residual was 0.03% of injected mass per timestep.

Those are the reported results for the 100 held-out branching cases. The largest breakthrough-time error was 4.3% relative to the converged finite-volume reference, and the largest reported cellwise residual was 0.03% of injected mass per timestep. Both figures are maxima, not averages.
Does 4.3% describe every branching case?
No. It describes the maximum breakthrough-time error across the 100 held-out cases. The statement does not give the error for each case or describe how the errors are distributed.
And is the 0.03% figure one residual averaged over the whole domain?
No. It is a maximum *cellwise* residual, expressed as a percentage of injected mass per timestep. Describing it as a domain-wide average would change the reported quantity.
Do the two maxima necessarily come from the same case?

The reported figures do not say. The case with the largest breakthrough-time error could be the same as, or different from, the case containing the largest cellwise residual. No case-level pairing is provided.
How should I state the denominator for the residual without making it sound like a percentage of total injection over the full run?
Say “0.03% of injected mass per timestep.” That retains the reported timestep scale. Calling it a percentage of cumulative injected mass over an entire run would use a different denominator.
Does “maximum cellwise residual” specify which cell had that value?
No. It reports the largest cellwise residual but does not identify the cell or its location. It also does not provide a spatial map of the other residuals.
Can I infer how many cases had breakthrough-time errors close to 4.3%?
No. A maximum identifies the upper observed value, not how many errors were near it. The statement gives no count, median, or distribution of breakthrough-time errors.
What is the scope of the observation?
It covers the 100 held-out ChannelShift-2D branching cases. The reported maxima describe that evaluated set; they do not provide results for other channel topologies or settings.
Is the 0.03% value a breakthrough-time error expressed in different units?

No. The 4.3% figure is a breakthrough-time error. The 0.03% figure is a cellwise residual normalized by injected mass per timestep. They describe different quantities, even though both are written as percentages.
Does the report give the breakthrough times themselves?
No. It gives the maximum percentage error in breakthrough time, not the individual surrogate or converged finite-volume breakthrough times.
Can I call these measured comparison results rather than another proposed evaluation?

Yes. This statement reports values obtained across the 100 held-out cases: a 4.3% maximum breakthrough-time error and a 0.03% maximum cellwise residual on the stated injected-mass-per-timestep scale. It does not give additional case-level measurements.
Please give me a compact results sentence that preserves both maxima and their scope.

Across 100 held-out ChannelShift-2D branching cases, the maximum breakthrough-time error relative to converged finite-volume solutions was 4.3%, while the maximum cellwise residual was 0.03% of injected mass per timestep.
Let’s advance the graph-mobility surrogate to broader connectivity testing. The held-out branching cases met both the mass-balance and breakthrough thresholds.

That is a decision to continue testing the graph-mobility surrogate, supported by the fact that the held-out branching cases met both thresholds. It does not say that broader connectivity testing has already been performed or that its outcomes are known.
What exactly is being advanced?

The graph-mobility surrogate—the approach using graph-predicted face mobilities with conservative finite-volume updates. The decision advances it to broader connectivity testing, rather than declaring the entire generalization goal settled.
Does the decision depend on both thresholds, or is the breakthrough result enough on its own?

The stated reason includes both: the held-out branching cases met the mass-balance threshold and the breakthrough threshold. Describing the decision as based only on breakthrough would omit part of its explicit basis.
Can I say that the surrogate has passed the held-out branching evaluation?
Yes, if you make the scope clear: the held-out branching cases met both specified thresholds. “Passed” should not be stretched into a claim about connectivity that has not yet been tested.
Remind me what the two thresholds refer to, without turning this into a new results report.

The mass-balance threshold concerns the maximum cellwise error staying below 0.1% of injected mass per timestep. The breakthrough threshold concerns error below 5% relative to a converged finite-volume solver on unseen channel connectivity. The decision says the held-out branching cases met both; it does not report results from broader connectivity testing.
Is broader connectivity testing just another name for the held-out branching test?

No. The held-out branching cases are the evaluated cases cited as the reason for the decision. Broader connectivity testing is the next testing stage to which the surrogate is being advanced. The decision does not specify which additional connectivity patterns that stage will contain.
Should I name a particular new topology in the decision?

Not unless it is specified separately. This decision says “broader connectivity testing” but does not identify particular additional topologies, a case count, or a test protocol. Naming any of those here would add details to the decision.
Does ‘advance’ mean we have committed to deploying the surrogate?
No. It means moving the surrogate forward to broader connectivity testing. Testing is the stated next stage; deployment is not part of this decision.
Could I characterize the held-out branching result as proof that it generalizes across all unseen permeability connectivity?

That would go beyond the decision. Meeting both thresholds on the held-out branching cases supports advancing the surrogate, but the stated next step is broader connectivity testing precisely as a further evaluation. The decision makes no claim about every unseen connectivity pattern.
Does the word ‘broader’ establish how much broader the next testing will be?
No. It indicates an expansion beyond the held-out branching evaluation, without specifying its size or coverage. The decision establishes the direction of the next test, not its detailed scope.
Would it be fair to say that local conservation and timing were both considered in making the decision?

Yes. The explicit reason is that the held-out branching cases met both the mass-balance and breakthrough thresholds. That keeps local balance and breakthrough timing distinct while recognizing that both informed the decision to advance.
Is the decision itself a claim that those thresholds will remain satisfied in the broader tests?
No. It states that they were met in the held-out branching cases and chooses broader connectivity testing as the next step. Whether either threshold is met under that broader testing remains open.
I want to avoid making the decision sound tentative when it is already made. How should I phrase that?

State the action directly: “Advance the graph-mobility surrogate to broader connectivity testing.” Then give the stated reason: “The held-out branching cases met both the mass-balance and breakthrough thresholds.” The uncertainty concerns future test outcomes, not whether this advance has been decided.
Can the reason be expressed without repeating individual error measurements?

Yes. Saying that the held-out branching cases met both thresholds fully expresses the reason given in this decision. Individual measurements are not needed to state the decision, and the wording should not imply that any broader-testing measurements exist.
What distinction should remain clear in a short closing sentence?

Keep the demonstrated scope separate from the next action: both thresholds were met on the held-out branching cases, and the graph-mobility surrogate is being advanced to broader connectivity testing. Do not describe that next testing stage as already completed or its thresholds as already met.

No. The bundle includes finite-volume references, but does not state that it contains solver settings, convergence records, or instructions for reproducing those references.

No. “Bundle” names a collection of materials; the description specifies its contents but not their storage format or presentation. In particular, it lists cellwise residuals, not a particular map or plot format.
Could I describe the per-case breakthrough errors as flux-split errors at junctions?
No. Breakthrough errors measure a timing discrepancy. Junction flux-split errors would measure something different, and they are not listed among this bundle’s specified contents.
Does the artifact assign an injected-mass-per-timestep normalization to the cellwise residuals?

Not in its description. It lists cellwise residuals without specifying values, units, a denominator, or a timestep convention. Those details should not be added as though they were part of the artifact definition.

No. It names cellwise residuals but reports no maximum or threshold finding. Having local residual data and establishing the numerical mass-balance condition are different claims.
